title: Using AI to Investigate an Emissions Variance | Validere
summary: When facility emissions run ahead of an internal target pace, learn what records to check, where AI can assist, and what requires human review.
body_markdown:
At a hypothetical oil and gas facility, year-to-date calculated emissions are running ahead of the pace used to track an internal emissions target. The environmental team needs to determine whether the gap reflects actual operating activity, an error in the source data or the emissions estimate, or a problem with the comparison itself. This is an investigation of an internal emissions target, not a permit variance or a finding of noncompliance.


## What does it mean when facility emissions are above the target pace?


Being above the target pace does not establish whether operating conditions changed, whether the target reflects current operations, or whether an input or calculation is incorrect.


Before investigating individual sources, confirm that both figures cover the same reporting period, use consistent units, and include the same emissions sources. An emissions total that includes only combustion cannot be compared directly with a target pace that includes combustion, venting, and fugitive emissions.


The methodology also matters. An updated emissions factor, or a change in methodology, can change the emissions estimate even when the facility operates the same way. If the target pace uses a different methodology or emissions factor, the team needs to understand how that difference affects the comparison. That does not automatically make the current inventory wrong or require a return to the older methodology.


The purpose is to explain the year-to-date result against that pace, not forecast where emissions might end up under a different operating plan.


## Which emissions and operating records should you check?


Once the figures are comparable, examine each source's calculated emissions and the records used to produce them. Check whether changes in operating activity, inputs, or methodology affected the emissions estimate.


What to examine


Question for the reviewer


Comparison and source records


Which sources show changes against a relevant reference, and are the figures being compared on the same basis?


Activity and operating history


Did fuel consumption, throughput, runtime, or other operating conditions change?


Methods and data quality


Did an input, an emissions factor, the methodology, or a data-quality issue affect the estimate?


Start by identifying which sources show meaningful changes in operating activity or calculated emissions against an appropriate reference, rather than ranking sources by their total emissions.


A compressor might account for a large share of the facility's emissions while its fuel consumption and calculated emissions remain consistent with comparable operating periods. A smaller source might show increased fuel use or longer runtime. The compressor contributes more to the total, but the smaller source may provide a better starting point for investigating the facility gap.


For a source showing higher calculated emissions, the team needs to determine whether the increase came from operating activity, a methodology change, or an incorrect input. Higher fuel consumption, longer runtime, and increased throughput may explain an operational increase. A changed emissions factor or incorrect input may instead affect the estimate without a corresponding change in operations.


The team must also distinguish a source-level increase from its contribution to the facility's gap against the internal target. If the target pace exists only as a facility-wide figure, changes in individual sources can help identify likely drivers. They do not automatically establish how much of the gap each source accounts for. Quantifying those contributions requires a defensible source-level comparison or attribution method.


## What problems can automated data checks identify?


Rules-based checks can flag missing required inputs, duplicate activity records, or values outside predefined thresholds. Those conditions are examples of[where rules-based automation fits better than AI](https://blog.validere.com/ai-environmental-compliance-workflows) .


For a flagged duplicate, check whether the record was used to calculate the emissions total. If it was never included, it cannot explain an increase in that total. If it was included, the team needs to establish its effect before correcting the result.


Statistical methods can also identify unusual patterns in operating history or differences between comparable equipment. These checks do not necessarily require generative AI. Whether a flagged pattern helps explain the facility's emissions gap still depends on the supporting records.


## How can AI help investigate emissions above target?


The records needed to investigate an emissions variance may be spread across emissions calculations, operating systems, activity logs, and data-quality reviews. When those records are accessible, an AI-assisted review might bring a source's emissions estimate together with its fuel consumption, runtime, calculation history, and quality flags. Where relevant operator notes or review comments are accessible, AI may also help summarize that information alongside the numbers.


Reviewing these records together can help the team distinguish changes in operating activity from changes in how emissions were estimated. Operator notes may provide context for an increase in runtime, while calculation records can show whether an emissions factor or methodology changed during the period. AI can help bring that information into the same review, but the reviewer still needs to verify each observation against its source.


AI may help identify promising lines of investigation, but it cannot establish a source's contribution to the facility's target gap without an appropriate comparison. Its observations do not replace the governed emissions calculation or authorize an inventory correction.


## When should the team correct the emissions inventory?


An emissions result that exceeds an internal target pace does not automatically need correcting. The appropriate action depends on what the records establish.


If the comparison uses inconsistent dates, emissions boundaries, or methodology, the team first needs to make that comparison valid. A problem with the comparison does not necessarily mean the inventory is wrong.


If operating records support a real increase in emissions and the calculations are correct, the team documents the explanation and retains that result. Changing the inventory simply to bring it in line with the target would misrepresent the facility's emissions.


If the investigation instead identifies a duplicate activity record or an incorrect input that affected the emissions total, the team verifies the issue before correcting the affected records or inputs and recalculating the result through the governed process. The correction should preserve what changed, why it changed, and the resulting emissions value.


## How should the emissions investigation be documented?


Someone reviewing the result later should be able to see which figures were compared, which activity data and methodology records were examined, and why the team retained or corrected the emissions value. A summary kept separately from those records may not provide enough information to reconstruct the investigation.


An investigation is easier to review when the source records, supporting context, and resulting decision stay connected to the emissions workflow. For more on Validere's approach, explore[AI in environmental operations](https://www.validere.com/ai-and-data-strategy) .
